title: Asher Yatzar
hookLine: a blessing after the bathroom thanks God for a body whose openings work

lines: NOT WHERE YOU'D LOOK FOR HOLY.
cards: The bathroom is not where people go looking for holiness. In, out, wash the hands, back to the day. Unless something goes wrong.

Ask anyone who's had kidney stones, or a bowel obstruction, or a newborn in intensive care who can't yet feed and digest on their own. Then you learn fast how much has to go right, every hour, without you asking.
Jewish tradition has a blessing for exactly this, said after using the bathroom. Today: Asher Yatzar.

teach.b: Asher yatzar means who formed. The blessing comes from the Talmud, and it's said after you've washed your hands.
It praises God, who formed the human being with wisdom, and created in us openings and openings, hollows and hollows.

Then it says something startlingly frank: it's known before your throne of glory that if one of them were opened, or one of them were blocked, it would be impossible to survive and stand before you even for a short while.
It ends by blessing God, who heals all flesh and acts wondrously. Openings and hollows: pipes, valves, tubes, chambers. The rabbis looked at the plumbing of the human body and called it wisdom.
Some doctors have written about how differently it reads after you've cared for patients whose bodies stopped doing these ordinary things.
The Psalms say something similar, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I will give thanks unto Thee, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made."

What makes Asher Yatzar unusual is where it puts the wonder. Not in a sunset or a mountain, but in one of the plainest things a body does, several times a day. Jewish tradition doesn't split the body off from the holy.
You don't have to be at your most spiritual to bless.

You just have to notice that it worked, again. For people living with illness, the blessing can be harder, or it can become a daily thanks for whatever still works. Either way, it's honest about how fragile a body is.

how: After using the bathroom and washing their hands, observant Jews say Asher Yatzar; it is also part of the morning blessings, and some homes hang the text near the bathroom door.

o: a prayer asking God to heal someone who is ill
a blessing after the bathroom for a body that works
a thanks said for the food you're about to eat

games.q: you're one of the rabbis composing blessings for everyday life. where do you put a blessing for the wonder of the body?

games.why: after the bathroom: one of the plainest things the body does, several times a day, is where the blessing sits.

practice: Feel your breath go in and out without your help, and your heart, if you can, and think of what's happening inside you right now: digesting, filtering, pumping, healing a scratch you forgot about.
If something in your body doesn't work well, you can hold that honestly too. Then say a quiet thank you for what did work.

wordCard.voice: Asher Yatzar. Who formed: the blessing after the bathroom for a body of openings and hollows that work, and for the one who heals all flesh.

orig.note: Hebrew: who formed. yatzar is the verb used when God forms the first human from dust in Genesis 2.

carryVoice: Your line: the body is a wonder. Even its plainest parts, several times a day. Until tomorrow.
